explanations.explanation: Yes, the horn is a run-for-cover signal. The cry says, “Assemble yourselves and let us flee to the fortified cities.” Nobody is told to stop and think it over. When that horn blows, the walls are the plan.

explanations.answer: March out and face the army
explanations.explanation: The text points the other way. The cry is to flee to the fortified cities, and verse 6 adds, “Seek refuge! Do not delay!” I'll admit I've charged at plenty of problems in my day, mostly cookie dough, but this horn says run for the walls. Nobody is told to face anything.

explanations.answer: Gather at the temple to pray
explanations.explanation: The people do assemble, but look at where they're headed. The cry says, “Assemble yourselves and let us flee to the fortified cities.” The destination is a fortified city, not the temple. Verse 8 does bring in mourning and wailing, but the horn call is about getting to safety.

The LORD says the opposite. In verse 6 He says, “For I am bringing disaster from the north, and terrible destruction.” That “…I am bringing…” is plain and personal. So the disaster doesn't come without Him, because He says He is bringing it.

Right, because the LORD speaks up about His part. He says, “For I am bringing disaster from the north, and terrible destruction.” He doesn't hide behind the army or the lion. The text puts the disaster in His own words.

Yes, and the verse is blunt about it: “He has left his lair to lay waste your land.” The cities will be reduced to ruins and lie uninhabited. A lion that leaves his lair isn't out for a stroll. I think this is the heaviest picture in the whole passage so far.
Peace is not on this lion's schedule. Verse 7 says he left his lair “…to lay waste your land.” and that the cities will be reduced to ruins and lie uninhabited. The word in the text is destruction.

explanations.answer: Pass it by on his way
explanations.explanation: This lion isn't passing through. The verse says he has set out and left his lair to lay waste the land. He has a target, and it's Judah. The text gives no hint of him walking on by.

Yes, verse 8 says, “So put on sackcloth, mourn and wail…” Sackcloth is what you wear when the heart is heavy. Nobody is picking an outfit for style here. The reason given is that “…the fierce anger of the LORD has not turned away from us.”

Armor would be for fighting, and the call here isn't to fight. The people are told to put on sackcloth, mourn and wail. Back in verse 5 the horn told them to flee, not to suit up. I can't picture anyone grabbing armor when the word is mourning.

No crowns in this verse. Verse 9 says the king and officials will lose their courage, and that's a long way from a coronation. What the people are told to put on is sackcloth, and then to mourn and wail. That's a day for mourning clothes.

Yes. Jeremiah says the people were told, “You will have peace…” while a sword is at their throats. Look at the gap between the promise and the sword. Peace was the word they heard, and the sword was the danger Jeremiah saw.

Victory sounds like something you'd hear before a battle, but it isn't the word here. Jeremiah says the people were told, “You will have peace…” while a sword is at their throats. The sword is the real picture in his words. Peace is what they were promised.

Riches never come up in this verse. Jeremiah says the people were told, “You will have peace…” while a sword is at their throats. A sword at the throat makes a person care about staying alive, not about money. The word he gives is peace.

The text says exactly the reverse. This wind blows “but not to winnow or to sift; a wind too strong for that comes from Me.” When I sift flour, it's a gentle shake over the bowl. This wind is too strong for that kind of job.

Yes, verse 11 says the wind blows “…but not to winnow or to sift…” Verse 12 adds, “…a wind too strong for that comes from Me.” Then the LORD says, “Now I also pronounce judgments against them.” So this is no gentle sorting job.

Yes, verse 13 says, “His horses are swifter than eagles.” Eagles are about as fast as anything gets in the sky. Picture those horses outrunning them. I can't catch a cookie rolling off the counter, so this speed is way beyond me.

The verse actually says it: “His horses are swifter than eagles.” It also says he advances like the clouds and his chariots are like the whirlwind. Clouds, whirlwind and eagles are the pictures this verse uses. Speed is the point of the horses.

Yes, verse 14 says, “Wash the evil from your heart, O Jerusalem, so that you may be saved.” The call goes to the heart, not just to the surface. It comes with a question too: “How long will you harbor wicked thoughts within you?” The alarm is loud, but this word is for the inside.

Street dust is a surface job, and this call goes deeper. Verse 14 says, “Wash the evil from your heart, O Jerusalem, so that you may be saved.” I know a little about dust, since I spent years under it in the back of a junk drawer. But this washing is for the heart.

Altars don't come up in this verse. The call is, “Wash the evil from your heart, O Jerusalem, so that you may be saved.” It's about wicked thoughts inside, as the next line says. The washing is for the heart.

Yes, the LORD says they surround her “…because she has rebelled against Me…” The reason comes from His own mouth, so there's no guessing. The army surrounds her like men guarding a field. The text gives rebellion as the reason.

The text never says that. The LORD gives the reason in verse 17: “…because she has rebelled against Me…” No insulting king shows up anywhere in these verses. I'd rather stick with the reason He actually gives.

explanations.answer: Her walls were built too weak
explanations.explanation: Walls aren't mentioned as the problem. The LORD says she is surrounded “…because she has rebelled against Me…” The reason is about rebellion, not construction. A weak wall isn't the cause given.

explanations.answer: Bitter and piercing to the heart
explanations.explanation: Yes, the LORD says, “This is your punishment; how bitter it is, because it pierces to the heart!” Right before that He says, “Your ways and deeds have brought this upon you.” I think this one is heavy, so let's let it be heavy for a moment. The text makes it clear this isn't a small thing.
The text says nothing like that. The LORD calls it bitter, saying it “…pierces to the heart!” Nothing about it is light. This is one of the heavier lines in the passage.

Easy to bear doesn't match the words. The LORD says, “This is your punishment; how bitter it is, because it pierces to the heart!” That's a hard thing to carry. I think this is a line to hold quietly.

explanations.answer: The horn and the alarm of battle
explanations.explanation: Yes, the voice says, “For I have heard the sound of the horn, the alarm of battle.” That's why the heart is pounding and the voice can't stay silent. After that sound, anyone would be shaken. I think this person is hurting.
No choir shows up in this verse. The voice says, “…I have heard the sound of the horn, the alarm of battle.” That's a sound that makes a heart pound. Singing is not what's going on here.

Bells make me think of Ruby, one of my cookie cutter kids, but there are no bells here. The voice says, “…I have heard the sound of the horn, the alarm of battle.” It's a horn, and it's an alarm. The pounding heart makes sense once you know that.
Yes, the cry says, “My tents are destroyed in an instant, my curtains in a moment.” It doesn't happen slowly. That's a lot to lose that fast. I think this one stings.
The words point to speed, not years. The cry says, “My tents are destroyed in an instant, my curtains in a moment.” It's over almost as soon as it starts. That's what makes it so heavy.
A winter would be slow, and this isn't slow. The cry says, “My tents are destroyed in an instant, my curtains in a moment.” The whole thing is sudden. I think that suddenness is what hurts.

Yes, the LORD says, “They are skilled in doing evil, but they know not how to do good.” It's a hard thing to hear, and He says it about people He calls His own. Just before, He calls them “…foolish children, without understanding.” I think this is a sad line.

Business never comes up here. The LORD says, “They are skilled in doing evil, but they know not how to do good.” The skill He names is a heavy one, and He says it about people He calls His own. I think that's what makes the verse sting.

Battle is all around this chapter, but it isn't the word here. The LORD says, “They are skilled in doing evil, but they know not how to do good.” The skill He points to is evil. That's the part that matters.

Yes, the one speaking says, “I looked at the mountains, and behold, they were quaking; all the hills were swaying.” Mountains are supposed to be the steady things. When they shake, nothing feels safe. This is a scary picture.
That's the opposite of what's seen. The text says the mountains were “quaking” and all the hills were “swaying.” Mountains are meant to be the steady ones. Here they aren't.
There's no sunshine in this scene. Verse 23 says the heavens “…had no light.” and verse 24 says the mountains were quaking and the hills swaying. It's dark and unsteady. Nothing about it is bright.
The text says the opposite. The one speaking says, “I looked, and no man was left; all the birds of the air had fled.” The land isn't full, it's empty. The birds are gone too.

Yes, verse 25 says, “I looked, and no man was left; all the birds of the air had fled.” Not even the birds stayed. It's a very quiet and empty scene. I think that quiet is part of what makes it heavy.

Yes, verse 26 says, “I looked, and the fruitful land was a desert.” What was once fruitful is now dry and bare. The cities are “…torn down before the LORD, before His fierce anger.” It's a hard thing to see.
A forest is a different picture from what's seen. The verse says, “…the fruitful land was a desert.” The land that was fruitful has become a desert. That's the change the verse points to.
A marsh is wet, and this picture is dry. The text says, “…the fruitful land was a desert.” What was fruitful has become empty. That's the change the verse points to.

Look at the little word that comes right after the hard part. The LORD says, “The whole land will be desolate, but I will not finish its destruction.” So He does not say He will finish it completely. That “but” matters.

Yes, the LORD says, “The whole land will be desolate, but I will not finish its destruction.” The desolation is real, and so is the limit He names. He doesn't say how or why here, so I won't guess. I'll just hold onto what He actually said.

explanations.answer: No He will not turn back
explanations.explanation: Yes, the LORD says, “I have spoken, I have planned, and I will not relent or turn back.” Those are firm words. He says the earth will mourn and the heavens will grow dark. He is clear and He is not changing course.

explanations.answer: Yes if the people beg Him
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't open that door here. The LORD says, “I have spoken, I have planned, and I will not relent or turn back.” Begging isn't mentioned in this verse. I'll stick with what He said.
One more warning isn't promised in these words. The LORD says, “I have spoken, I have planned, and I will not relent or turn back.” He says He won't relent. That's all the verse tells us.
Yes, verse 29 says, “Every city is abandoned; no inhabitant is left.” First they flee into the thickets and climb among the rocks. Then the cities sit empty. That's a very still picture.

The verse says it plainly: “Every city is abandoned; no inhabitant is left.” The people flee at the sound of the horseman and archer. They go into the thickets and among the rocks. Nobody is left in the cities.

Yes, verse 30 says, “your lovers despise you; they want to take your life.” All the scarlet, the gold jewelry and the eye paint don't change that. The text says she adorns herself in vain. Dressing up can't fix this.
Admiring isn't what the text says. It says, “your lovers despise you; they want to take your life.” The scarlet and gold don't win them over. The text says she adorns herself in vain.
Pity would be a softer thing, and the text is harder. It says, “your lovers despise you; they want to take your life.” That's a long way from pity. It's a hard verse.

Yes, the Daughter of Zion cries, “Woe is me, for my soul faints before the murderers!” She is gasping for breath and stretching out her hands. I think this is one of the saddest cries in the passage. Let's let it be sad.

Priests did show up earlier, in verse 9, where they tremble in fear. But the cry at the end is different. The Daughter of Zion says, “Woe is me, for my soul faints before the murderers!” That's the word she uses.

Prophets also showed up in verse 9, where they're astounded. But in this cry the Daughter of Zion says, “Woe is me, for my soul faints before the murderers!” That's the word at the end. It's a heavy one.
